lens: mobile task completion, visual hierarchy, accessibility, and recovery

findings.observation: The responsive route exposes labeled controls, a modal dialog with focus trapping and focus return, reduced-motion behavior, dark mode, text alternatives, and no horizontal overflow at 375, 390, 844-landscape, 1024, and 1440 pixels. A real screen-reader session and browser zoom matrix beyond the simulated 200 percent root text check were not available.
findings.evidence: Playwright browser runs on 2026-08-08; output/playwright/relationships-mobile-390-final.png; reduced-motion dialog animation and transition were both 0.00001 seconds; Lighthouse accessibility 100; ten visible mobile controls measured at least 44 by 44 pixels.
findings.user_impact: The critical path is structurally accessible, but a screen-reader or switch user could still encounter an ordering or announcement problem that automated inspection cannot prove absent.
findings.recommendation: Run VoiceOver or an equivalent screen reader through Today, evidence review, revision, dismissal, People, and Searches before treating this as release-level accessibility proof.
findings.verification: Complete the critical path using only screen reader and keyboard input; identity, source, proposed state, consequence, and every decision must be announced once in visual order, and focus must return to the invoking control.

findings.observation: The final production desktop Lighthouse run scored 97 performance with 2.2 second LCP, while the mobile-throttled run scored 92 with 3.0 second LCP and 150 millisecond total blocking time. The mobile LCP is the marketing hero heading, not the relationship workspace.
findings.evidence: output/playwright/lighthouse-relationships.json and output/playwright/lighthouse-relationships-mobile.json generated against a clean production Next.js server on 2026-08-08.
findings.user_impact: The product concept remains responsive after load, but slower mobile connections may delay the first meaningful page heading enough to weaken perceived quality.
findings.recommendation: Profile route-level global CSS and shared client JavaScript, then defer below-fold relationship concept code where it does not compromise server-rendered meaning.
findings.verification: Repeat mobile Lighthouse and a throttled browser trace three times; median LCP must be at most 2.5 seconds, CLS remain 0, and no product interaction may be delayed or removed.

strengths: The desktop evidence sheet uses the Shadcn-compatible Radix dialog primitive for semantic naming, inert background, focus trapping, Escape dismissal, and exact focus return.
The route switches cleanly to the existing phone concept below 900 pixels and shows no horizontal overflow at 375, 390, or 844-landscape viewports.
A simulated 200 percent root text size preserved the mobile product without horizontal overflow; a discovered footer overflow was corrected and retested with no remaining offender.
All ten visible mobile product buttons measured at least 44 by 44 pixels in the 200 percent text scenario.
Light, dark, reduced-motion, long mixed-script identity, missing avatar, empty search, no-action, and unresolved-identity states were directly inspected.
Final production Lighthouse scored 97 performance and 100 each for accessibility, best practices, and SEO on desktop; mobile scored 92 and 100/100/100.
missing_evidence: Repeated mobile performance traces after route-level CSS and JavaScript profiling.
Real-device browser safe-area, virtual-keyboard, and touch ergonomics.
Simplified Chinese localization expansion and RTL behavior.
open_questions: Should the public route load only the currently applicable desktop or mobile product implementation to reduce below-fold code on slower devices?
Which mobile state should remain visible when a recruiter returns after an interruption in the authenticated product?
